newsitem.title: FRANCE: Year after death, Mitterrand evokes muted praise. [CORRECTED 14:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Year after death, Mitterrand evokes muted praise. [CORRECTED 14:35 GMT]

text.p: A year after his death, memories of President Francois Mitterrand evoked only muted praise from his political heirs and old foes in ceremonies on Wednesday.
Conservative President Jacques Chirac sent a vice-admiral to lay a wreath at the tomb in Jarnac, southwestern France, of the Socialist head of state who died of cancer after ruling for 14 years.
But the ambivalence of Mitterrand's legacy was summed up by Socialist Laurent Fabius, one of his former prime ministers.
"There were good things and bad things and...the Left will have to learn lessons from the mistakes," said Fabius describing his old boss as "calculating".

Opinion polls show that a small majority of French people regard Mitterrand favourably, praising him for cutting the working week, lowering the pension age to 60 from 65 and abolishing the death penalty.
But his image has been tarnished over the past year by allegations that he misled France for more than a decade by hiding his cancer. He had come to power in 1981 promising openness about his health.
The riverside town of Jarnac has drawn some 300,000 people over the past year, boosting local commerce as pilgrims tour his birthplace and lay his trademark red rose at the tomb.
In a short speech, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin dubbed him "a formidable fighter" but singled out corruption scandals which clouded his legacy.

"We didn't all react the same way. Some people loved him to the point of being faithful on everything. Others, like me, had enough esteem for him to be able to tell him what they did not approve of," Jospin said.

Former Foreign Minister Roland Dumas, chief keeper of the flame as head of the Institut Francois-Mitterrand, called on Parisians to lay a red rose outside the building where Mitterrand died on January 8.
But no political truce marked the anniversary.
Conservatives accused Mitterrand's heirs of exploiting it in the run-up to parliamentary elections due early next year. (Corrects from "early this year".)
"People are still enthusiastic about Mitterrand," Dumas retorted. "Whether or not some people, let's be honest about it, are shifting their stance ahead of (the elections) is a side issue," he said.
Chirac's office has denied a report by author Georges-Marc Benamou that Mitterrand despatched an aide in late 1994 to urge Chirac to stand in the May 1995 presidential election.
Benamou wrote in "Le Dernier Mitterrand" (The Last Mitterrand) that he acted out of "visceral hatred" for Chirac's fellow-conservative rival, Prime Minister Edouard Balladur.

Mitterrand's close aide Michel Charasse said he did not know if the report was true, but added in an interview with the daily France-Soir that in November 1994 he was sent to tell Chirac: "Do tell him that I wish him no harm."

The biggest tribute to Mitterrand will focus on his legacy and draw Cuban President Fidel Castro and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat among others to a seminar at the U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, former U.N. secretary-general Boutros Boutros-Ghali and Israeli ex-Prime Minister Shimon Peres are also expected to attend the January 9-10 symposium.
